newsitem.title: UK: Can BMW jump-start Rover to profitability?.
newsitem.headline: Can BMW jump-start Rover to profitability?.

text.p: When Rover Group first met BMW, it may have been love at first sight for the British company, but the German car giant had only one thing on its mind -- Land Rover's attractive profit margins.

The courtship was even captured on film for a British television documentary. Now three years into their union, Rover is about to deliver its first new product from the relationship -- a "baby" Land Rover.

The Freelander is the result of the injection of billions of dollars of BMW's money and world-renowned technical know-how into Rover. The launch next year will be key to BMW's objective to make Rover Group profitable by the year 2000.
"Freelander will be a major factor in whether we hit that target," said Bernard Carey, Rover board member and director of external affairs.

"Every new product is vital to achieving that ambition. But it is particularly so with Freelander because it's not replacing a model. It is a new product and market for us to be in," he said in an interview.
Arthur Maher, head of research at LMC International, sister motor analyst to the influential J D Power, agrees that the Freelander could make or break Rover's turnaround.

"Freelander is going to be fundamental ... Land Rover is the jewel in the crown of the Group. The 4x4 division has done very well with Discovery but Land Rover is looking for the next improvement in sales and product," he said.
"This is particularly important to BMW as it looks to take on Mercedes' new M class (of 4x4 vehicles) which is new, more upmarket, prestigious and close in pricing to LR products," Maher added.
Freelander will fill a crucial gap in Land Rover's vehicle portfolio. In recent years offroaders have seen good growth in Europe, but more so in the United States.
One of the fastest growing sub-divisions in the sector has been the smaller offroader or sports utility vehicle.

As other manufacturers were scooping up sales, LR was losing out. Bill Baker, Land Rover's newly appointed director of corporate affairs and one of the key figures involved in the strategic launch of Freelander, summed up:
"The reason we developed Freelander was because there was this key sector of less expensive, lighter vehicles and we weren't in it.

"Freelander had started out using technology from the car side of the business. But as it developed it had more Land Rover capabilities built into its brief and now has some off-road capability." Baker told Reuters.
Baker, a former vice president of Land Rover North America, said Freelander would be priced at between $24,500 and $34,300, with three- and five-door models available.
The Freelander will be launched in Britain in January and then roll out to Europe, eventually being sold in South Africa, Australia, Southeast Asia and eventually Japan.
"We see it attracting a younger buyer, one who is successful but not yet at the peak of their earning capability. The three-door will appeal to the singles market and the five-door to couples."

Rover sources expect first-year European sales to be between 35,000 and 50,000 Freelanders. Outside Europe the target is 10,000 to 20,000, with 4,000 to 5,000 expected to be sold in its Japanese debut year.
